titleNl: Waar heb je die laptop gekocht?
titleEn: Where did you buy that laptop?
intro: In this college you'll learn how to shop in Dutch: talk about clothes and sizes, give your opinion on second-hand items, ask for your money back, and return a parcel or online order using the perfect tense.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — shopping and the past tense
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme nine. Its title is a real, everyday question: [[Waar heb je die laptop gekocht?]], which means 'Where did you buy that laptop?'. Notice that this sentence is about the past, about something you already did. In Dutch we often say the past with the perfect tense, and that is the grammar heart of this whole theme. You take a small form of the verb [[hebben]], 'to have', and you put a special past form right at the end of the sentence. So 'I bought it online' becomes [[Ik heb het online gekocht.]] Hear the shape: [[Ik heb]] near the front, and [[gekocht]] at the very end. That word [[gekocht]] means 'bought', and you will use it constantly in shops. Today we learn clothes and sizes, how to ask for a refund, how to talk about second-hand things, and how to return a parcel. As always, I explain everything in clear English, but every Dutch word you hear is spoken by a native voice, so your ear gets trained too. Please repeat each Dutch phrase out loud after me — that is how it sticks. Are you ready to go shopping? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Clothes and what to wear
paragraphs.text: Let's start with clothes, in Dutch [[kleren]]. The most useful pieces are: a coat, [[de jas]]; trousers, [[de broek]]; a shirt, [[het overhemd]]; a dress, [[de jurk]]; a sweater, [[de trui]]; and shoes, [[de schoenen]]. To say 'I am wearing' something, use the verb [[dragen]]. For example: [[Ik draag vandaag een warme jas.]], 'today I am wearing a warm coat'. In a shop you will need sizes. The word for size is [[de maat]], and the key question is [[Heeft u dit in maat 40?]], 'do you have this in size forty?'. If something does not fit, you say [[Deze broek past niet goed.]], 'these trousers don't fit well'. Maybe it is too small, [[te klein]], or too big, [[te groot]]. You might also want a different colour, [[een andere kleur]]. A very polite way to ask to try something on is [[Mag ik dit even passen?]], 'may I try this on for a moment?'. The fitting room is called [[de paskamer]]. And to ask the price, you simply say [[Wat kost deze jas?]], 'what does this coat cost?'. These few sentences already let you handle almost any clothes shop with confidence.

paragraphs.heading: deze, die, dit and dat — pointing at things
paragraphs.text: When you shop, you point at things all the time: 'this one', 'that one'. Dutch has four little pointing words, and which one you use depends on the word's gender and on near or far. For close things use [[deze]] and [[dit]]; for things further away use [[die]] and [[dat]]. With 'de' words you use [[deze]] for near and [[die]] for far. Because 'coat' is a 'de' word, you say [[deze jas]] for 'this coat' and [[die jas]] for 'that coat'. With 'het' words you use [[dit]] for near and [[dat]] for far. Because 'shirt' is a 'het' word, you say [[dit overhemd]] for 'this shirt' and [[dat overhemd]] for 'that one over there'. You will hear them in real questions like [[Wat kost deze trui?]], 'what does this sweater cost?', and [[Is die broek in de aanbieding?]], 'are those trousers on sale?'. You can even point without a noun: [[Ik wil deze, niet die.]], 'I want this one, not that one'. A handy tip: if you forget the gender, most learners just say [[die]] or [[dat]] and Dutch people still understand you perfectly. Pointing plus a smile gets you a long way.

paragraphs.heading: The perfect tense — talking about what you did
paragraphs.text: Now back to our star grammar: the perfect tense, for talking about the past. The recipe is simple: a form of [[hebben]] plus a past participle at the end. The forms of 'to have' are [[ik heb]], [[jij hebt]], [[hij heeft]] and [[wij hebben]]. For regular verbs the participle is 'ge' plus the stem plus 't' or 'd'. So 'pay', [[betalen]], becomes [[betaald]]: [[Ik heb de jas online betaald.]], 'I paid for the coat online'. 'Order', [[bestellen]], becomes [[besteld]]: [[Ik heb het online besteld.]], 'I ordered it online'. But watch out — many shopping verbs are irregular and you just learn them. The most important is 'buy', [[kopen]], which becomes [[gekocht]]. So our title sentence is [[Waar heb je die laptop gekocht?]]. Two more very common ones: 'bring' becomes [[gebracht]], and 'get' becomes [[gekregen]], as in [[Ik heb mijn geld terug gekregen.]], 'I got my money back'. Hear the pattern again: the helping word stays near the front, the participle drops to the end, like in [[Ik heb gisteren een broek gekocht.]], 'yesterday I bought trousers'. Make a tiny list of these participles and say them daily; they appear in almost every conversation about the past.

paragraphs.heading: Refunds, receipts and second-hand opinions
paragraphs.text: Sometimes a purchase goes wrong, so you need refund language. The golden sentence is [[Ik wil graag mijn geld terug.]], 'I would like my money back'. You can also ask [[Kan ik mijn geld terugkrijgen?]], 'can I get my money back?'. If a thing is broken, you say [[Het is kapotgegaan.]], 'it broke', or [[Het doet het niet meer.]], 'it doesn't work anymore'. Two cultural musts here. First, always keep your receipt; the receipt is [[de bon]] or [[de kassabon]], and the staff will often ask [[Heeft u de bon bewaard?]], 'did you keep the receipt?'. Second, in many shops you cannot get cash back but you can swap the item; 'to exchange' is [[ruilen]], so you say [[Ik wil deze broek graag ruilen.]]. Now, opinions about second-hand clothes, in Dutch [[tweedehands kleding]], which is very popular and normal in the Netherlands. You might say [[Ik koop mijn kleren graag tweedehands.]], 'I like buying my clothes second-hand', because [[het is goedkoper en beter voor het milieu]], 'it is cheaper and better for the environment'. Or you can disagree: [[Ik koop liever nieuwe kleren.]], 'I prefer to buy new clothes'. Both opinions are completely fine to share.

paragraphs.heading: Returning a parcel — a mini-scenario
paragraphs.text: Finally, let's return an online order, which happens to everyone. Your parcel is [[het pakket]], and 'to send back' is [[terugsturen]]. Often it is free: [[U kunt het gratis terugsturen.]], 'you can send it back for free'. In the perfect tense the word joins together, so 'I have already sent it back' is [[Ik heb het al teruggestuurd.]]. Most returns in the Netherlands go via [[PostNL]], so listen for that name. Now imagine the scene. You bought shoes online, but they are too small. You go to the shop counter and say: [[Goedemiddag, ik heb deze schoenen online gekocht.]] You explain the problem: [[Ze zijn te klein. Ze passen niet.]] The salesperson asks [[Heeft u de bon?]], and you answer [[Ja, hier is de bon.]] Then you say what you want: [[Ik wil graag mijn geld terug, alstublieft.]] The reply is warm: [[Geen probleem, ik regel het.]], 'no problem, I'll sort it out'. You finish with [[Dank u wel, fijne dag nog!]]. See how the perfect tense, the pointing words and the refund phrases all work together? Practise this little dialogue out loud today. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I'll see you in theme ten!
